summary.text: Antibiotic resistance is when bacteria change so that antibiotics no longer work to treat infections, and it is one part of the wider problem of antimicrobial resistance.
It arises through spontaneous mutation, horizontal gene transfer, and the pressure of antibiotic overuse in both medicine and agriculture.
The World Health Organization calls antimicrobial resistance one of the top global public health threats and warns of up to 10 million deaths a year by 2050 unless action is taken.

items.prompt: A doctor prescribes antibiotics for a condition they cannot treat. What wider risk builds up when this happens often?

options.label: Bacteria become easier to treat over time
The drugs lose their effect only in the patient
Resistance spreads faster through overprescribing
Only farm animals are affected, not people

items.explain: Overprescribing and inappropriate prescription of antibiotics have accelerated resistance, and many prescriptions are unnecessary.

items.prompt: Random mutations are rare. Why do they still matter so much in microbes that reproduce quickly?

options.label: Frequent, rapid reproduction raises the chance some gain a helpful mutation
Fast reproducers cannot repair any of their mutations
Mutations in fast reproducers are never rare at all
Fast reproducers pass on only the helpful mutations

items.explain: Although random mutations are rare, many microbes reproduce so often and so rapidly that some members are likely to acquire one that increases resistance.

items.prompt: A hospital says a patient has become resistant to a drug. Where does the resistance actually sit?

options.label: In the patient's body, which has learned to ignore the drug
In the microbe causing the infection, not the patient
In the drug, which has weakened over time on the shelf
In the hospital's hygiene, which has let the infection thrive

items.explain: Resistance is a property of the microbe, not of the person or other organism it infects.

items.prompt: Which step is aimed at reducing the spread of resistance?

options.label: Prescribing antibiotics for every cough as a precaution
Using more antibiotics on farms to stop infections
Stopping all new work on antibiotic research
Using narrow-spectrum antibiotics and better hygiene

items.explain: Preventive measures such as narrow-spectrum antibiotics and improved hygiene aim to reduce the spread of resistance.

items.prompt: A few bacteria in a large population happen to shrug off a drug, and the drug keeps being used. Over time, which kind becomes more common?

options.label: The easily defeated ones, since the drug favours them
Both kinds in equal numbers, as the drug has no effect
The naturally protected strains, since the rest are cleared
Neither kind, because the whole population dies off

items.explain: Strains with natural resistance become much more prevalent than the ones that are easily defeated by medication.

items.prompt: A newspaper says antibiotic resistance is a problem for the future. What did a WHO report say instead?

options.label: It is limited to a few hospitals in rich countries
It is happening now in every region of the world
It only affects people who are very old or very young
It will start only after the middle of this century

items.explain: The WHO report stated that this serious threat is no longer a prediction for the future but is happening right now in every region of the world.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Antibiotic resistance is when bacteria change so that antibiotics stop working for the people who need them to treat infections. It is one part of a wider problem, antimicrobial resistance, in which microbes evolve ways to protect themselves from the drugs used against infections in humans, animals and plants. A resistant microbe is one that a drug could once treat but now cannot. Resistance belongs to the microbe, not to the person or other organism it infects.

paragraphs.heading: Kinds of resistance
paragraphs.text: Any microbe can become resistant, so alongside antibiotic resistance there is antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic resistance. For bacteria, resistance is split into two kinds. Microbiological resistance, the most common, comes from mutated or inherited genes that let bacteria withstand the way an antibiotic kills them. Clinical resistance shows up when treatment fails, because bacteria that are normally beaten by it survive and become resistant. Microbes that resist many drugs are called multidrug-resistant, and sometimes superbugs.

paragraphs.heading: How it arises
paragraphs.text: Resistance comes from spontaneous mutation, from horizontal gene transfer, and from the selective pressure of antibiotic overuse in medicine and farming. Mutations that occur during cell division are rare and random, but many microbes reproduce often and fast, which raises the chance that some member of a population gains one that helps it resist. Under that pressure, either microbes evolve a defence, or strains with natural resistance become much more common than the easily killed ones. Resistance does arise naturally over time, but antimicrobial use inside and outside healthcare has made it more and more common.

paragraphs.heading: Passing genes along
paragraphs.text: Bacteria that have gained resistance can hand the genetic cause of it to other bacteria through horizontal gene transfer. This happens in three ways: conjugation, transduction and transformation. Such sharing lets resistance spread through one species of pathogen, and even into similar bacterial pathogens.

paragraphs.heading: Too many prescriptions
paragraphs.text: Misuse and overuse of antimicrobials largely drive the problem, and overprescribing and inappropriate prescribing of antibiotics have sped it up. About 154 million antibiotic prescriptions are written every year, and up to 46 million of them are unnecessary or wrong for the patient's condition. As many as 1 in 3 antibiotic prescriptions may be unneeded. At the same time, many people have no access to essential antimicrobials.

paragraphs.heading: The human cost
paragraphs.text: The World Health Organization counts antimicrobial resistance among the top global threats to public health and development. It estimates that resistant bacteria directly caused 1.27 million deaths in 2019 and contributed to more than 4 million in 2021. One in five people who died because of it were children under five. Resistant infections are harder to treat and often need costly alternative therapies that may have worse side effects. The WHO and other bodies warn of up to 10 million deaths a year by 2050 unless action is taken.

paragraphs.heading: Fighting back
paragraphs.text: Steps to slow the spread include using narrow-spectrum antibiotics and better hygiene. Global efforts, such as calls for international treaties on the problem, push for less misuse, more research funding and access to needed drugs in developing nations. The COVID-19 pandemic pulled money and scientific attention away from the issue, making the challenge harder.
